To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the British Mandate for Palestine's Chief Justice Michael McDonnell was a liberal-minded, Irish nationalist, Catholic who, as a British civil servant in a settler-colonizing state, identified with its Arab Palestinian subject-population, and who, in his judicial role, upheld the supreme, independent, impartial judiciary against the Executive's attempts to subordinate it to political expediency.

the appointment of an Irish Chief Justice to Mandatory Palestine in 1927 led to a clash between the Irishman's insistence on impartial justice and the British government's desire to use the courts to further its political agenda.

The main takeaway from our work is that

the British Empire's colonial justice system in Palestine was not a neutral arbiter of competing claims but a tool for managing conflict in favour of British interests, which were not always those of the settler community, as in this case.

the history of the Irish in the British Empire is not simply a story of Irishmen serving as imperial agents, but of the ways in which Irishmen, and Irishwomen, were also agents of change in the British Empire.

the Irish Catholic experience in British Palestine, and the British Empire more generally, was not one of simple colonialism, but of a complex, multi-layered, and often conflicted experience that was both shaped by and in turn shaped the British Empire.
